A brand archetype report & differentiation strategy for Hannah · Collins + Adeline Designs
Brand Archetype Report Identity · Voice · Landscape · Differentiation · Visual Direction · October 2026
What this report is: the result of your brand archetype assessment, scored on Skyway’s weighted 37-point engine across all twelve archetypes, then translated into identity, voice, a read of your market, and a visual direction. Every number in it comes from answers you gave; the second tab holds those answers exactly as you submitted them.
01 · Brand Identity

The jeweler who starts with an idea, not an inventory.

Your result is a close three. Creator leads at 8 of 37, with Magician and Jester level at 7 a single point behind, and the engine reads a one-point lead as a pairing rather than a verdict. What it adds up to is a design house: something imagined, made into a piece that changes the moment it is given, by a brand that would rather be anything than dull.

Creator · 8 · Innovation
The idea is the product

You described a jewelry design company that offers its own designs and custom pieces. The making came first in your own sentence, before the selling.

  • Your motto, “if it can be imagined, it can be created,” is the Creator’s, word for word.
  • You reward the people who “generate fresh, creative, out-of-the-box ideas.”
  • Faced with a problem, you “turn problems into inspiring works of innovation.”
Magician · 7 · Power
The piece changes the moment

A stone and some metal become the thing a person is remembered by. That is a transformation, and your answers kept reaching for it.

  • Asked for the brand’s character, you chose “mystical and transformative.”
  • “Captivating” is among your three strengths, and your ambassador is the dragonfly, the Magician’s animal.
  • Your purpose, “to leave a mark on the world,” and your symbol, a key, both sit in the Magician’s family.
Jester · 7 · Enjoyment
Anything but dull

You never called the brand funny. You told us what it cannot stand, which is a stronger signal.

  • Two of your three fears are the Jester’s: boredom and negativity.
  • Those two words carry six of the Jester’s seven points. None of your strengths or self-descriptions is a Jester answer.
  • In fine jewelry that shows up as wit and surprise. It never shows up as jokes.

At the core, you’re a Creator.

The Creator’s drive is Innovation: the conviction that a thing worth having does not exist yet and ought to. Your motto says it outright, and two of the three heaviest questions in the assessment, what you reward and how you meet a problem, both came back Creator. All eight of your Creator points come from those three answers about how you work. That makes this a particular kind of jeweler. Most online diamond sellers start with a stone and ask the customer to pick a setting for it. You start with the idea and go looking for the stone it needs. Lean into: the sketch, the named design, the piece that did not exist until someone asked for it.

Magician and Jester: your twin influences, level at seven.

These two are tied to the point, so neither outranks the other and each gets a job. The Magician is the effect: what a piece does once it leaves you. You called the brand mystical, transformative and captivating, and you want it to leave a mark. The Jester is the spark. It arrives through your fears, boredom and negativity, which makes it a standard rather than a style: nothing dull leaves the bench, and nothing in the brand sells by making a woman feel she is lacking something. Lean into: the moment a piece marks, a quick line of wit where the category goes hushed, and delight treated as part of the design brief.

Why the combination is one-of-a-kind.

The twelve archetypes group into four families by core human drive, and your three leaders come from three different ones: Creator from Structural, Magician from Legacy, Jester from Connector. The fourth family, Spiritual, holds 2 of your 37 points. The largest family is not the one your lead archetype sits in. Legacy carries 14 of 37, and it is the family whose purpose you chose word for word: to leave a mark on the world. So the making is the method and the mark is the motive. One more reading sits in the zeros. Sage and Caregiver both scored nothing, and those are the two archetypes online diamond retail is built on: the seller who educates and the seller who reassures. You are neither, and Part II is built around that opening.

The one thing to make unmistakable
Any diamond site can show her ten thousand stones. Only a design house can show her the drawing. You are selling what was imagined, and the stone is where it starts.
“If it can be imagined, it can be created.”
Your own answer, and the Creator’s motto verbatim — the identity in one line
One register sits underneath: Ruler. Asked to picture the brand, you chose the Executive over the Artist, and the pillars of an estate over a museum. Ruler scored only 2, but both of those points are about how the brand looks, and they agree with every style word you gave us: classic, elegant, luxurious. Composure is the room. Imagination is what happens in it.

The guardrail: Creator leads; Magician and Jester sit level beside it. Be imaginative without being precious, enchanting without going mystical, and witty without telling a joke. If a line could sit on any diamond retailer’s homepage, it is the wrong line.

Creator · how you work

Your motto, “if it can be imagined, it can be created.” The people you reward, who “generate fresh, creative, out-of-the-box ideas.” Your approach to problems: “we turn problems into inspiring works of innovation.” Three questions about method, three Creator answers, eight points. Whenever the assessment asked how you work, the answer was the same.

Magician · what the work does

Brand character: “mystical and transformative.” A strength: “captivating.” Ambassador: the dragonfly. Add a purpose of leaving a mark and a key for a symbol, and the Magician is how the brand describes itself whenever it is asked for a picture instead of a process.

Jester · what you refuse

Your fears were boredom, negativity and incapability. The first two are the Jester’s, and they supply six of its seven points. You were offered “fun-loving and humorous” as a character and “entertaining” as a strength, and took neither. This Jester does not perform. It guards the door against the dull and the dour.

Where the engine disagreed with you

Three questions ask you to place the brand in a family. You chose Legacy twice, with “to leave a mark on the world” and a key, and Connector once, with the red-into-purple gradient. The scoring put Creator first, which sits in Structural, so the check reads 0 of 3. The gap is narrower than the number. Your three picks are exactly the families of Magician and Jester. You place the brand by why it exists; the engine scored how it works. Both are true, and it is one to confirm with you on review.

03 · Core Purpose

Turn what she can imagine into the mark she leaves

You exist for the woman who wants the piece nobody else at the table is wearing. She is thirty to fifty-five, she already buys well online, and a catalogue of ten thousand near-identical rings is exactly what she is trying to get away from. You take what she can picture, or what you pictured for her, and make it real in stone and metal. Then it does what good jewelry has always done. It marks the promotion, the wedding, the year she got through, and one day it belongs to someone who will ask where it came from.

It is the Creator’s purpose, if it can be imagined, it can be created, pointed at the Legacy family’s reason for existing: to leave a mark on the world.

Alternates to react to

A diamond is found. A piece is imagined.

Made once, for one woman, and then for whoever she leaves it to.

04 · Voice & Personality

Speak like the woman who designed the ring she’s wearing.

If the brand were a person: the best-dressed woman at a long dinner in a house with columns out front, who drew the ring on her hand herself and will tell you how in two sentences. She notices what you are wearing and asks about it. She is quick, a little wicked, and never at anyone’s expense. She does not explain carat weight unless you ask, and when you ask she is exact.

Imaginative

We are inventive, exacting, design-first  ·  not trend-led, catalogue-flat, or precious about process.
“It began as a ribbon coming undone. It took four drawings to get the knot right.”

Captivating

We are evocative, assured, a little spellbinding  ·  not mystical, breathless, or horoscope copy.
“Some pieces mark the moment. This one tends to cause it.”

Quick

We are witty, warm, knowing  ·  not jokey, cute, or emoji-led.
“Yes, it goes with everything. That is rather the point of a diamond.”

Simple

We are spare, composed, exact  ·  not stiff, hushed, or luxury-by-adjective.
“One stone. One line of gold. Nothing left that we could take away.”

On the dials: designed over sourced · wit over whimsy · spare over ornate · certain over eager · romantic, but never sentimental.

Product page

“Named for the garden gate it was drawn from. One oval, set low, on a band fine enough to disappear.”

Custom enquiry reply

“Tell us what you keep picturing. A sketch on a napkin is plenty. We’ll send drawings back before we talk about stones.”

Social post

“Nobody ever inherited a ring and said, how sensible.”

The guardrail: wit is seasoning. One light line per page at most, and none on the pages where she is deciding whether to trust you with a diamond she has not held: sizing, returns, shipping, certification. Those pages are plain and exact.
Part II · The Strategy

Now that we know who you are, here’s how you win.

An identity only matters if it opens a lane the competition cannot follow you into. So we started with the two rivals you named, mapped the national online market around them, and looked for the position none of them can hold.

05 · Competitive Landscape

Three camps. None of them own your lane.

Scoped to your stated reach, which is national and online, and starting from the rivals you named, the market sorts into three camps: the diamond marketplaces, the mission brands, and the modern jewelers. Each is strong at one thing and built in a way that keeps it from being the others. (Read from each brand’s public positioning in October 2026, and to be validated with you on review.)

Camp One
The diamond marketplaces
WhoBlue Nile, now absorbing James Allen under Signet; Ritani; Rare Carat Our readSage + Everyman. Selection, price and education at scale Voice“The original online jeweler”; trustworthy, transparent, technology-first; unbiased education guides and a standing offer to match a rival’s price You winThey sell a stone and a spec sheet, and they will match the price on it. Do not meet them there. A filter can find her a diamond. It cannot imagine her a ring.
Camp Two
The mission brands
WhoBrilliant Earth, VRAI, Clean Origin Our readCaregiver + Sage. Provenance, sustainability and proof of conscience Voice“Ethically sourced fine jewelry,” “Beyond Conflict Free,” annual mission reports, percentages of repurposed gold You winThey made where it came from the reason to buy. By now every site in the category says “responsibly sourced” in nearly the same words, and she cannot tell the claims apart. You make what it is the reason to buy.
Camp Three
The modern jewelers
WhoRing Concierge, Frank Darling, Mejuri, Catbird Our readEveryman + Lover, with a Jester streak. Fine jewelry made casual and everyday Voice“For women, by women”; “no gatekeeping”; “jewelry you can live in”; a showroom that feels like a friend’s living room You winThey took fine jewelry off the pedestal. Your buyer wants hers back on one: exclusive, distinctive, a little grand. They make the everyday piece. You make the one she is known for.
The open lane
A design house with an estate’s composure and a spark the category would never risk. Original, grand and never dull, all at once.

The marketplaces can configure a ring but cannot originate one. The mission brands lead with conscience, so the design arrives second. The modern jewelers have the personality and spent it on making fine jewelry casual. Nobody in the three camps is design-first, formal in register and light on its feet at the same time. One caution: Signet has said it will reposition Blue Nile as “elevated luxury,” so the upmarket end of this map is about to get more crowded. The answer is to be the designer, which is the one thing a marketplace cannot become.

06 · Differentiation Strategy

Five ways to pull away

Each pillar targets the open lane, and each is something the brand should actively say rather than quietly imply. A pillar any competitor could also claim has been left out.

Lead with the drawing, not the diamond.

Every camp opens with the stone: carat, cut, colour, clarity, certificate. They say it in the same words, and a buyer has no way to referee one retailer’s “exceptional quality” against another’s. So quality has stopped working as a reason to choose. A design has not. It is visible in a thumbnail, it cannot be price-matched, and it is what you scored highest on. Your motto is a design promise, and nobody in the three camps opens with one.

In the brandGive every piece a name, a one-line origin, and its sketch beside the finished photograph. Product titles are names first and specifications second. Of your two working taglines, “Rare by Design” is this pillar in three words. “A Legacy of Grace” gets the family right, but grace is poise, and your answers are about imagination and never being boring. One check before you commit: a diamond marketplace already trades as Rare Carat, so clear the line with a trademark search first.

Make custom the front door.

“If it can be imagined, it can be created” is a custom-design promise. The marketplaces answer it with a configurator: pick a setting, pick a stone. The modern jewelers answer it with an appointment in a city showroom. You sell nationally from Olney, Illinois, with the occasional pop-up, so your custom process has to work for a woman in Dallas who will never meet you. That is worth solving in public, because a visible, named process is itself the proof that a piece is being made for her.

In the brandName the process and show its stages: the conversation, the drawings, the render, the making. Publish three finished commissions from first sketch to finished piece. Put the motto on that page, where it is a promise you can be held to.

Sell the mark, not the everyday.

Your stated purpose is to leave a mark on the world, and Legacy carries 14 of your 37 points. The modern jewelers sell the opposite idea: jewelry to live in, for every day. The mission brands sell a clear conscience at the point of purchase. Neither is talking about what the piece becomes in thirty years. That is the Magician’s ground. A piece from you is the first page of a history, and the brand should behave as if it knows that.

In the brandPut a record card in every box: the name of the piece, the date it was finished, and who it was made for. Offer engraving wherever the design allows. Write about pieces in the future tense as readily as the present.

Answer her six worries as a maker, not a teacher.

You listed them yourself: authenticity, quality, security, sizing, returns, and whether the piece looks as luxurious in person as it does online. The category answers these with education libraries and mission reports, which is the Sage and the Caregiver at work. You scored zero on both, and trying to out-teach Blue Nile would cost you the identity. Answer as a Creator and show the thing. A hand, daylight, movement and scale settle the last worry faster than any paragraph, and it is the worry a design-led brand is best placed to settle.

In the brandOn every product page: the piece on a hand in daylight, a few seconds of it moving, and a four-line block covering what is certified, how it ships, how it is sized and how it comes back. Treat each pop-up as proof, and film it. Keep price out of the headline. You named it as a difference, but the marketplaces will match a figure, and price is not on the list of things you told us she values.

Be the one house in the category that is never boring.

Boredom and negativity are two of your three fears. They are also a fair description of how much of the category sounds: reverent, anxious, or, in the word one modern jeweler’s co-founder used for the big online names, “beige.” The modern camp fixed that by going casual. You can fix it without lowering the register, because wit in a formal room is rarer and better remembered than wit in a living room. And the fear of negativity hands you a rule much of e-commerce breaks daily: never sell by shortage, shame or countdown.

In the brandOne line of wit per touchpoint, and choose the touchpoints: the inside of the box lid, the order confirmation, the care card, the names of the pieces. No countdown timers, no “don’t settle,” and no copy that makes her feel she is missing something.

Your strategic sweet spot
Heirlooms with a pulse.

A Creator’s imagination, a Magician’s sense of occasion and a Jester’s refusal to be dull, aimed at the woman who wants the piece nobody else has.

07 · Visual Identity · Concept Strategies

Three ways to look the part

Direction, not decoration: three strategic concepts, each true to Creator with Magician and Jester beside it, and each tested against the classical register you asked for. The designed colour boards and imagery come after you pick a direction.

Concept A
The estate

Composure first.

The setting you chose, built out: cream stock, deep moss, a gold-foil crest and a high-contrast classical serif. The brand arrives looking as if it has always been there.

Pros
  • Matches every style word you gave us
  • Foil-ready from day one, on a ring box or a card
  • Gives a fresh brand instant standing
Tradeoffs
  • A crest in green and gold is one of the most claimed looks in luxury
  • All register, little imagination: it shows the Ruler’s 2 points and hides the Creator’s 8
  • A new house in an old house’s clothes can read as costume
Concept B
The sketchbook

The drawing is the hero.

A design-house system. Cream paper, a fine drawn line, the sketch shown beside the finished piece, and gold only where it is real: foil on the box, metal in the photograph.

Pros
  • Tells the Creator story on sight
  • Nobody in the three camps looks like this
  • Turns the custom process into the content
Tradeoffs
  • Needs a real drawing for every piece, every time
  • Reads as studio rather than luxury if the photography is weak
  • Less overtly romantic at first glance
Concept C
The night garden

Enchantment, with a wink.

The plate, extended: deep moss as the ground, cream as the light, rose as the flash, and the dragonfly as a recurring creature. Jewelry seen at dusk instead of under showroom lights.

Pros
  • The most ownable of the three, and the most Magician
  • Gives rose and moss a clear job each
  • The dragonfly carries real jewelry lineage, back to Lalique and Art Nouveau
Tradeoffs
  • Dark grounds are hard on diamond photography, so product needs its own neutral stage
  • Tips into fairy garden if the illustration turns literal
  • Furthest from the classical look you described

The color thinking

You were drawn to rose #D0697F, cream #F4EDDC and moss #7C8A46, steered away from tangerine, violet and marigold, and asked to keep gold as an element that can be foiled onto a ring box. Two of those look like contradictions and are not. You avoided marigold and asked for gold: the answer is that gold is a material here, never a colour. It appears as real foil and as real metal in photographs, never as a flat printed yellow. You chose the red-into-purple gradient and avoided violet: that question measures drive, not palette, and your rose sits at its red end, so keep the purple end out. On the archetype, the instinct holds. Cream is the Creator’s page, a deepened moss is the Magician’s dusk, and rose is the Jester’s flash. Two checks before it is signed off. Sector: a diamond is a small mirror and takes on whatever surrounds it. Rose behind a white stone pinks it on screen, and moss throws a green-yellow cast that an informed buyer reads as a lower colour grade. Your own list of buyer worries ends with whether the piece looks as luxurious in person as online. So product is always shot on cream or neutral grey, and rose and moss live in packaging, type and campaign imagery, never within reflection distance of a stone. Resemblance: rose with gold foil is the blush-and-gold of a decade of direct-to-consumer brands aimed at women, and it reads mass-market, which is the one thing your buyer is avoiding. Rose and moss at equal weight read florist or wedding stationery, and a notch more saturation makes them seasonal. Deep green with a gold crest on a box reads as a watch box from across a room; Rolex has owned that pairing for decades. The mitigation is ratio and temperature: cream dominant, moss taken down to a near-black olive and kept yellow-leaning instead of emerald, rose held under a tenth of any surface, and gold confined to foil. One useful accident: nothing in your palette comes near the category’s blues, from Tiffany’s box to Blue Nile’s name, so you will not be mistaken for either.

The type thinking

You asked for classical and high contrast, and your style words are classic, elegant, luxurious and artistic. Three of those four point at the same face, and it is the one every bridal and fashion brand already uses: the hairline Didone of magazine mastheads. It would be correct and anonymous. The fourth word, artistic, is the Creator asking for evidence of a hand. So choose a high-contrast serif with some calligraphy left in it. Playfair Display or Instrument Serif do the job from the free shelf, and Fraunces adds a soft, slightly wayward italic that is the Jester’s wink in type; Canela, Ogg or Saol Display are the licensed upgrades. Set it against a quiet sans for everything functional, such as Instrument Sans, Mulish or Archivo. One production note, because you want this foiled on a ring box: hairlines break up or fill in under hot foil at small sizes, so the wordmark needs a sturdier cut drawn for the lid as well as the elegant one for the screen. And treat the plus sign as the one custom glyph in the name. Neither of your named rivals has one, and it can stand alone as a stamp on the smallest surface you own.

One flag before the swan is drawn: a swan has been the emblem of Swarovski for decades, and it kept the bird through its last rebrand. In jewelry specifically, a swan on a box lid risks being read as crystal at fashion prices, which is the mass-market signal your buyer is avoiding, and it is a trademark question to put to counsel before a foil die is cut. There are two ways through. Keep the swan but make the crest the mark, with the bird drawn as fine line engraving inside it and never as a lone silhouette. Or look again at the creature you chose unprompted, the dragonfly. It is the signature animal of Art Nouveau jewelry, we did not find it in use by any brand on this map, and its four wings give you the gemstone and plain variants you asked for. It needs the same clearance search. We would sketch both.
Our lean: Concept B, dressed in Concept A’s materials. A design-house system where the drawing leads, carried on cream stock with classical type and real gold foil, so it has the composure you asked for and the imagination you scored. Borrow one thing from Concept C: let the dragonfly live inside the box lid or in the tissue, where she finds it after she has opened everything else. That is the Jester, and it costs almost nothing.
08 · Summary

A Creator’s imagination, with a Magician’s touch and a Jester’s spark.

Design is the product, transformation is what it does, and the refusal to be dull is the standard it is held to, with an estate’s composure setting the room. In a market split between marketplaces that sell the stone, mission brands that sell the conscience and modern jewelers that sell the everyday, you are the house that sells what was imagined, and makes it to be handed down.
